[
693
]

I am satisfied that these disadvantages can be
lessened, if not completely overcome. I note that neither extended family nor
friends seem to form a large part of these children’s day-to-day lives.
Technological advances will assist in maintaining these connections, if a move
takes place.

[
694
]

Ms. J.D.1 can facilitate Skype access between
the children, Mr. S.D. and other family members.  Any concern that the use of
technology would present a problem for religious reasons has been allayed by Ms.
J.D.1’ testimony that she and Rabbi P.S. developed their own relationship
through frequent use of Skype meetings. I am confident that they will
understand the need to make similar efforts to ensure that the children have
access to technology, so that they can maintain their connection with their
father, friends, and other family members in Canada.

[
695
]

This brings us to the achingly difficult crux of
the matter. There is no doubt that the biggest disadvantage of the move, by
far, is the loss of frequent in-person contact with their father.  For all his
faults, there is no question that Mr. S.D. loves his children, and they love
him.

[
696
]

Ms. J.D.1 does have a plan for the children to
have extended visits with their father during school breaks, if they move to
England.  Although, there are concerns about how this family can afford access trips
for four children, if those issues can be overcome, it may be that the benefit
to the children of having peaceful time with each parent, without the intrusion
of constant conflict, may outweigh the loss of frequent contact.  Frequent
contact is a good thing but only if it is healthy.  In this family, thus far,
it has not been.

[
697
]

Difficult though it is to consider moving the
children so far away from their father, it is clear that the current situation
cannot continue. Mr. S.D.’s access is now reduced to five hours of supervised
contact per week, due to his breaches of court orders and continued failure to
protect the children from his feelings about Ms. J.D.1 and Rabbi P.S.. This is
not a healthy long-term solution for this family.

[
698
]

Mr. S.D. has been given several warnings and
chances to improve his behaviour, so that he could resume a more normal access
schedule with his children. He has been unwilling, or unable, to do so. We need
to try something new.

[
699
]

These children have had to endure the toxic
relationship between their parents since separation. It has been horrible and
it is not in the children’s best interests to remain in this situation any
longer. Despite the obvious love
between Mr.
S.D. and the children, their relationship is not a positive contribution to
these children’s lives.  The benefits of starting a new life in England, away
from the upsetting exposure to Mr. S.D.’s instability, far outweigh the benefits
of remaining in Toronto to maintain their current situation and their contact
with their father.

[
700
]

I agree with Ms. J.D.1 that the move may even
open up possibilities that will strengthen the relationship between Mr. S.D.
and his children.  Perhaps, once the power struggle between these parents has
been removed, and Mr. S.D. does not have to deal with Ms. J.D.1 and Rabbi P.S.
on a regular basis, he will be able to focus on enjoying his time with his
children. If they visit with him in the summer, as Ms. J.D.1 proposes, Mr. S.D.
will be able to act as their primary parent for extended periods.  Ideally, the
children will be able to settle in for a more relaxed and normal day-to-day
life with him during visits, without rushing and constantly having to go back
and forth between their parents’ homes.

[
701
]

My hope is that, for the first time in their
lives, these four children will be able to experience peace when they are with
each parent.

[
702
]

Until now, their father, in particular, seems to
have been parenting at his lowest possible level.  The battle with Mr. S.D. has
also caused Ms. J.D.1 to behave inappropriately at times, both with Mr. S.D.
and others, such as school personnel. In short, both parents appear to bring
out the worst in each other.

[
703
]

It is my fervent hope that this new arrangement
will present a better opportunity for Ms. J.D.1 and Mr. S.D. to be the best
parents they can be for J.A.P., L.A.D., H.A.D. and S.B.D.. These children
deserve no less.

Decision
about mobility

[
704
]

I am satisfied that the advantages of the children
moving to England with their mother outweigh the disadvantages.

[
705
]

Ms. J.D.1 will be permitted to move with the
children once three conditions have been met:

a.

She needs to obtain a custody order between her
and Mr. D.P., and an order in those proceedings permitting her to move J.A.P.
to England.

b.

She needs to provide proof that immigration
officials in England have approved her and the children moving to England.

c.

JFCS

needs to be satisfied that the
relationship between Rabbi P.S. and the children has improved sufficiently that
it is no longer a protection concern.

[
706
]

Once Ms. J.D.1 has satisfied these conditions,
her counsel should provide proof to Mr. S.D.’s counsel (or if none, to Mr. S.D.).
If there is a dispute about whether the proof adequately addresses the
conditions, Ms. J.D.1 may bring a 14B motion on notice to Mr. S.D..  He will
have two weeks after he is served to file responding material.  If the
presiding judge in Newmarket is unable to make a decision on the written
material about whether the conditions have been met, he or she may remit the
matter to me for decision or further direction.

ACCESS

[
707
]

I realize that this order is going to be
terribly upsetting to Mr. S.D..  Given his apparent inability to shield the
children from his emotions, it is not in their best interests to be in Mr. S.D.’s
unsupervised care at this time.

The first visit

[
708
]

There will be an order that Mr. S.D.’s first access
visit after this decision is released is to be in the presence of a therapist
or counsellor approved by Ms. J.D.1 and the OCL. If Mr. S.D. needs help
locating a suitable person, perhaps the OCL or JFCS will be able to assist. If
there is a cost, it shall be paid by Mr. S.D.. The purpose of this visit is to
ensure that Mr. S.D. and the children have an opportunity for therapeutic
support, if necessary, during their first meeting after they know that they
will be moving. It is likely to be a challenging visit and it is important for
the children that supports be in place to minimize the stress on the children
and protect them from their father’s emotional reaction.

The next four visits

[
709
]

The next four visits are to be exercised at a
Supervised Access Centre or in the presence of a professional supervisor. As a similar
order is in effect now, I presume that the parties have settled on an
appropriate supervisor to ensure that the children are not being exposed to any
inappropriate behaviour or comments by Mr. S.D..

Ongoing visits

[
710
]

Mr. S.D. has indicated that he has been
attending for counselling to gain a better understanding of the effect of his
conduct on the children. If Mr. S.D. or his counsel provides Ms. J.D.1’ counsel
with proof, by way of a report through his therapist, that Mr. S.D. has been
attending therapy regularly and appears to appreciate the need to avoid
exposing his children to negativity about their mother, Rabbi P.S. or this
decision, Mr. S.D. should be permitted to attempt to resume unsupervised
access.

[
711
]

Initially, Mr. S.D.’s access will continue to be
from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. each Sunday. If four daytime unsupervised visits occur
without problems, Mr. S.D. may then resume exercising unsupervised access on
alternate weekends from after school on Friday to the beginning of school on
Monday.

[
712
]

The resumption of overnight contact is, in part,
to allow Mr. S.D. and the children as much time as possible together until the
move to England takes place.  However, if Ms. J.D.1 believes that Mr. S.D. is
continuing to expose the children to harmful behaviour during any of his
daytime or overnight unsupervised access, or if she receives any more
threatening or abusive communications from him, she may unilaterally make the
decision that any further access needs to be exercised at the Supervised Access
Centre until further order of the court.  Given Ms. J.D.1’ demonstrated
commitment to facilitating access in the past, I am satisfied that she is not
likely to abuse this power. She seems to understand that, for the children’s
sake, it is important that they have an opportunity to continue to see their
father, as long as he is behaving appropriately during access.

[
713
]

Either party may bring an urgent motion in
Newmarket, on at least four days’ notice to the other side, to determine any
access dispute.  If the presiding justice feels unable to deal with the matter,
he or she may try to arrange for the motion to be scheduled before me.

[
714
]

However, this is a Newmarket file and I do not
normally sit in Newmarket. Scheduling a motion before me will present some
logistical difficulties, so I declare that I am not seized with any post-trial
motions that either party may bring. All motions should be vetted by a
Newmarket judge, who may refer the file to me if he or she believes it is
necessary.

Access after the move

[
715
]

Once the children move to England, Mr. S.D. will
be entitled to a Skype access visit with the children each Sunday. Each of the
children is to spend a minimum of 10 minutes on the Skype call with their
father. The total Skype visit shall not exceed one hour. I am putting these
limits on the Skype calls as they may be unsettling for the children,
particularly at first, and because Mr. S.D. has used telephone access in the
past to be unduly intrusive into Ms. J.D.1’ parenting. The parties can arrange
a time that will accommodate the time difference between the two countries that
will not disrupt the children’s schedule. If the Skype access goes well, Ms.
J.D.1 may agree to expand it in the future, if she feels that would be in the
best interests of the children.

[
716
]

The parties are to exchange proposals about an
access schedule, so that the children have at least four weeks of access with
their father in Canada each year in even numbered years and five weeks of
access in odd numbered years.

[
717
]

If the parties do not agree on a schedule, the
children will spend four weeks of access with their father during the summer in
even numbered years. In odd numbered years, they will spend two weeks with
their father in Canada over each December school break (or the English
equivalent) and three weeks in the summer.

[
718
]

The summer access should not be for three or
four consecutive weeks, unless the parties agree otherwise.  As Ms. J.D.1 has
promised that she will travel to Canada with the children in the summer, she
should ensure that the children are in Canada for at least five weeks in even
numbered years and four weeks in odd numbered years. Ms. J.D.1 will be entitled
to schedule up to seven days of time with the children at some point during the
time that they are in Canada. This will allow the children to spend time with Ms.
J.D.1’ family and will ensure that the younger children, in particular, do not
have to go for too long a period without seeing their primary caregiver. Ms.
J.D.1 may select her choice of seven days, which need not be consecutive. She
is to notify Mr. S.D. no later than May 1 each year of the dates when the
children will be with her during summer access.

[
719
]

I cannot stress too strongly to Mr. S.D.: it is
up to him to make this access work. If the children continue to be exposed to
stress during his time with them, there will, no doubt, be a request that his
access be, once again, exercised in a supervised setting or completely
curtailed.

[
720
]

No one wants to take this step, particularly
when Mr. S.D.’s time with his children will be so limited. However, the court
is required to make access orders that are in the best interests of children.
It is unlikely that it would be in the children’s best interests to continue
access, if Mr. S.D. is upsetting the children or undermining their ability to
settle into their lives with their mother and Rabbi P.S. in England.

[
721
]

There will also be an order that, if Mr. S.D. is
able to travel to England and arrange accommodation, he may do so up to twice a
year and spend up to two weeks with his children while he is there, provided it
does not disrupt their schooling.

SUPPORT

[
722
]

I have already commented that it is impossible
to determine Mr. S.D.’s income, given his failure to provide disclosure and his
complete lack of honesty about his finances.

[
723
]

However, Ms. J.D.1 has not met the onus of
establishing that Mr. S.D. is making the $60,000 per year on which she would
like me to base his support obligations.

[
724
]

I understand Ms. J.D.1’ suspicions. Mr. S.D. was
able to provide his family of six with a reasonable lifestyle before
separation, which included a nanny, luxury cars, a gym membership and dining
out.

[
725
]

However, after separation, Mr. S.D. seems to
have fallen apart. He drifted between Montreal and Toronto, and I accept his
evidence that he was crying frequently and on medication for depression. His
presentation in the courtroom suggested that Mr. S.D. is struggling with a high
level of emotional dysregulation.

[
726
]

It is understandably difficult for Ms. J.D.1 to
accept Mr. S.D.’s evidence of poverty, when he provides her with minimal child
support, but was able to take at least one vacation, take the children to a
hotel with a waterslide, buy the two youngest children iPads and take all the
children out to eat at restaurants.

[
727
]

However, the reality is that Mr. S.D. has been
on Ontario Works and living with his parents for much of the time since
separation. There is no evidence to substantiate the claim on his financial
statement that he paid his parents $3,000 a year in rent. I find that it is
more likely than not that he did not pay his parents anything for rent or other
living expenses. If so, he could have had a little extra money from his social
assistance or other sources to take the children out occasionally or buy them
gifts. I also accept his evidence that his parents financed the trip to Niagara
Falls, so that the entire extended family could be together over the holiday
period. The evidence of Mr. S.D.’s lifestyle certainly does not satisfy me that
he was making $60,000 per year.

[
728
]

In terms of his recent attempt to establish a
business, Mr. S.D. does not appear to have either the skills or temperament to
make that business a success. We only know of two customers that he has had,
and neither of those jobs worked out.

[
729
]

I wish to be practical in establishing Mr. S.D.’s
arrears and ongoing support obligations. Despite his lack of disclosure, there
is little point in making an order that Mr. S.D. will never be able to pay.

[
730
]

I am prepared to base Mr. S.D.’s support
obligations on his lawyer’s submissions about what Mr. S.D. has been making
since separation. I recognize that this is being generous to Mr. S.D., as this
is the minimum income that would be reasonable to impute to him.

[
731
]

However, even these figures will result in Mr.
S.D. owing substantial arrears, which he will have difficulty repaying. There
is little utility in embarking on an exercise to try to impute a higher income
to him, given the lack of an evidentiary basis to make those calculations.

[
732
]

I accept Ms. Bhardwaj’s submission that Mr. S.D.
was on Ontario Works from shortly after the separation until the end of 2013. I
also accept her admission to Justice MacKinnon on January 21, 2015 that,
despite his 2014 Line 150 income of $8,055, Mr. S.D. earned $18,000 in 2014. I
accept that he was back on Ontario Works at some point but that his Social
Assistance income ended in April of 2015. I am prepared to accept Ms.
Bhardwaj’s submission that Mr. S.D. has made approximately $30,000 per year for
2015 and 2016.

[
733
]

Even without these submissions from counsel, I
would have imputed at least $30,000 per year of income to Mr. S.D., given his
evidence that he had a contract with Ms. Volaria for $86,000 and another with
Ms. Dibb for an initial price of $95,000. Although I recognize that the entire
contract price is not profit, it seems reasonable to conclude that Mr. S.D. was
capable of generating at least $30,000 of income from the time that he started
his business in April 2015.

[
734
]

However, given the difficulties that Mr. S.D.
has had with his business, I am prepared to limit Mr. S.D.’s imputed income to
the $30,000 per year of income that Ms. Bhardwaj suggested Mr. S.D. is capable
of earning.

[
735
]

Mr. S.D. should have been paying support since
separation. However, as he was on Ontario Works in 2012 and 2013, I find that
he would not have had the ability to pay support during those years beyond the
total of $400 or $500 that Ms. J.D.1 acknowledges Mr. S.D. gave to her for the
children.

[
736
]

On an income of $18,000 for 2014, Mr. S.D.
should have been paying $340 per month. As he has not provided any evidence
that he paid any support prior to Justice MacKinnon’s January 21, 2015 order,
this means that Mr. S.D. owes $4,080 in child support arrears for 2014.

[
737
]

Mr. S.D.’s actual or imputed income for 2015 and
2016 was $30,000. The table amount for four children under the
Child Support
Guidelines

is $725 per month.

[
738
]

At the end of the trial in January 2016, Ms.
J.D.1 acknowledged that she had received seven months of payments of $340 for a
total of $2,380.

[
739
]

This means that, as of January 15, 2016, Mr.
S.D.’s arrears are:

2014                                                                                        $4,080

January 2015 to
January 2016 (13 months x $725)                $9,425

Payments
$2,380

BALANCE
$11,125

[
740
]

Thereafter, Mr. S.D. should have been paying
$725 per month on an imputed income of $30,000 per year.

[
741
]

Mr. S.D. should receive credit for any payments
he has made since January 15, 2016, as well as for any additional payments he
can prove that he made for dates when support was accruing prior to that date,
which have not been included in the calculations above. This would
not
include
the $400 or $500 paid in October of 2013, as I have not imposed any support
liability for 2013.

[
742
]

Until Ms. J.D.1 and the children leave for
England, Mr. S.D. should continue to pay child support according to the
Child
Support Guidelines

of $725 per month.

[
743
]

However, once Ms. J.D.1 and the children leave
for England, this is an exceptional case for which it is appropriate to make an
order that is not in accordance with the
Child Support Guidelines
.
There
will be substantial access costs. Rabbi P.S. and Ms. J.D.1’ have said that they
will be able to provide the children with a higher standard of living in
England than Mr. S.D. would be able to provide them with here. The combination
of the access costs and Rabbi P.S.’s assurances about his financial resources
satisfies me that Mr. S.D. qualifies for a finding of undue hardship under
s.
10
of the
Child Support Guidelines.
I find that requiring Mr. S.D. to
pay $725 per month in support, as well as the travel costs for the children’s
access, would be an undue hardship and result in Mr. S.D. having a lower
household standard of living than Ms. J.D.1 and the children.

[
744
]

Under s. 7 of the
Child Support Guidelines
,
“special
or extraordinary” expenses are normally shared in proportion to the parents’
incomes. However, this is only a “guiding principle”. S. 7(1) does not require
the court to make an order for proportionate sharing. The wording of s. 7(1)
leaves the court with discretion about whether or not to award any additional
amount for s. 7 expenses.

[
745
]

This is an unusual case, which makes the usual
approach to s. 7 expenses difficult. I have no evidence about what extra expenses
the children will incur in England. Rabbi P.S. has assured the court that he
can provide for all the children’s expenses, if they move to England.  I have
no idea what either parent’s income will be, once the move takes place.

[
746
]

Requiring Ms. J.D.1 and Mr. S.D. to negotiate
about how much each of them should pay towards extra expenses, including
airfare for access, will invite a resumption of the conflict that the physical
separation is designed to eliminate.

[
747
]

I have decided to exercise my discretion in
apportioning s. 7 expenses by requiring Mr. S.D. to assume responsibility for
all of the access costs, in lieu of paying other special expenses and requiring
him to pay full
Guideline
support. This will give Mr. S.D. some
incentive to get back to work full-time to maximize his earnings, so that he
can pay for the children to come to visit him. It is my hope that this
arrangement will also allow Mr. S.D. to offer the children a reasonable
standard of living in his home, when they are visiting him for access.

[
748
]

I am not concerned that this order will result
in the children being unable to visit with their father. I have no doubt that Mr.
S.D. will find a way to fund these visits, either through his own earnings or any
remains of his $50,000 inheritance, or with the assistance of his family.

[
749
]

My order is that on the first day of the first
month after the move takes place, Mr. S.D.’s child support obligations will be
reduced to $600 (Canadian) per month. He will be responsible for the costs of
all of the children’s trips to Canada.

[
750
]

Ms. J.D.1 will be responsible for her own
airfare, as long as the children require an adult to accompany them. Ms. J.D.1
has assured the court she intends to come back to visit her family each summer,
in any event. It is appropriate that she pays for her own flight to do so, both
so she can maintain her family connections, and so that she can follow through
on her promise to ensure that the children have an opportunity to spend several
weeks with their father each year. That promise was a key component of her plan
that convinced the court to approve her plan. I am sure it will be very
important, should there be any future proceedings, that Ms. J.D.1 be able to
demonstrate that she has done her best to honour her promise.

CURRENT
SECTION 7 EXPENSES

[
751
]

The major expense for the children is the cost
of their private school tuition. Until the children leave for England, Mr. S.D.
should continue to be responsible for one-half of the schooling costs.

[
752
]

After the children move to England, Ms. J.D.1
and Rabbi P.S. should be responsible for the schooling cost. Rabbi P.S. has
said that he is prepared to assume this cost, and it is appropriate that he and
Ms. J.D.1 do so. Mr. S.D. will not have the same opportunity in England as he
does here to negotiate a reduction in the tuition due to his financial
circumstances. He will not be able to pay this cost, in addition to the $600
per month and the full transportation costs for the children to exercise
access.

SPOUSAL
SUPPORT

[
753
]

Mr. S.D. was the primary breadwinner for this
family during the marriage. He should have continued to provide support to his
children and Ms. J.D.1 after the separation. Ms. J.D.1 was entitled to spousal
support on both compensatory and noncompensatory grounds.

[
754
]

However, I find that Mr. S.D. was functioning so
poorly after the separation that he was barely able to support himself, let
alone pay spousal support to Ms. J.D.1. As she has always done, Ms. J.D.1 found
a way to survive and support herself and the children.

[
755
]

There would be no point in making an order for
retroactive spousal support. Mr. S.D. does not have the ability to pay it and
it would compromise his ability to pay his ongoing child support.

[
756
]

I also suspect that I may be asked to make a
substantial cost award against Mr. S.D. for this lengthy trial. There is no practical
advantage to adding to Mr. S.D.’s indebtedness with an award for spousal
support arrears. Given Mr. S.D.’s limited means since separation, his
retroactive child support obligations should come first.

[
757
]

I find that, after his child support obligations
are taken into account, Mr. S.D. did not have the ability to pay spousal
support to Ms. J.D.1.

[
758
]

Ms. J.D.1 has not asked for ongoing spousal
support.

RESTRAINING
ORDER

[
759
]

I am concerned about Mr. S.D.’s reaction to this
decision. He has shown that he has anger management issues, and he has been
threatening and abusive to both Ms. J.D.1 and Rabbi P.S..

[
760
]

Mr. S.D. has also demonstrated a troubling
pattern of allowing this dispute to intrude into the children’s schools.  He
insisted on attending the Hanukkah play despite the restraining order.  He
pulled J.A.P. out of class to discuss issues related to this litigation. He visited
the girls’ school to “get a hug” from the headmaster and talk to him about Mr.
S.D.’s personal issues with Ms. J.D.1. As Mr. S.D. is not to be in the presence
of the children without supervision, he should not be attending at their
schools.

[
761
]

The terms of the existing restraining order are
to continue. Additionally, Mr. S.D. is not to initiate communication with Ms.
J.D.1, except in the case of an emergency when the children are in his care. He
may respond to Ms. J.D.1, if she contacts him to discuss any matters related to
the children, but all communication is to be respectful and focus only on the
children. Absent an emergency, all communication should be in writing,
preferably by text or email. Ms. J.D.1 may demand that Mr. S.D. cease
communication at any time, and it will be considered a breach of the
restraining order if he fails to do so, after being given written notice.

CLOSING COMMENT TO COUNSEL

[
762
]

This has been a long and difficult case. I wish
to express my thanks to all counsel for their assistance. Despite the difficult
dynamics between the clients, counsel remained civil, focused and professional
throughout. They each fearlessly and tirelessly advocated for his or her
client, but remained courteous to both each other and the court. I am most
appreciative of their efforts, as should be their clients.

FINAL ORDER

Custody and Mobility

1.      All four children are to be placed in the sole custody of
their mother, J.D.1.

2.      Ms. J.D.1 is authorized to make all decision relating to the
children without input from Mr. S.D.. She is to keep Mr. S.D. informed of all
major decisions, including medical and educational decisions. She is to use her
best effort to provide Mr. S.D. with a copy of all report cards and progress
reports, academic or extracurricular awards, school or extracurricular
photographs, or similar documentary “markers” of significant events or
achievements in the children’s lives, as soon as possible after she receives
them.

3.      Paragraphs 3 and 5 of MacKinnon J’s January 21, 2015
endorsement are to be incorporated into the final order.

4.      Ms. J.D.1 may obtain passports, national identification and
any other documents for the children without Mr. S.D.’s consent. The children’s
passports, if still being held by the Newmarket court, are to be released to Ms.
J.D.1.

5.      Ms. J.D.1 may travel with the children, within and outside
of Canada, without Mr. S.D.’s consent. She is to keep him advised of the
children’s whereabouts and contact details, if they are going to be away from
their home for more than 72 hours.

6.      Mr. S.D. is not to travel with the children outside of
Ontario, without Ms. J.D.1’ consent, such consent not to be unreasonably
withheld.

Mobility

7.      Ms. J.D.1 will be permitted to move outside of Canada with
the children once three conditions have been met:

a.

Ms. J.D.1 needs to obtain a custody order
between her and J.A.P.’s biological father, D.P., and an order in her divorce
file with Mr. D.P. permitting her to move J.A.P. to England.

b.

Ms. J.D.1 needs to provide proof that
immigration officials in England have approved her and the children moving
permanently to England.

c.

Ms. J.D.1 needs to provide Mr. S.D. with written
proof that Jewish Family and Children’s Services

is satisfied that there
is no protection concern relating to the relationship between Rabbi P.S. and the
children.

8.      Once Ms. J.D.1 has satisfied these conditions, her counsel
should provide proof to Mr. S.D.’s counsel (or, if none, to Mr. S.D.).  If
there is a dispute about whether the proof adequately addresses the conditions,
Ms. J.D.1 may bring a 14B motion, on notice to Mr. S.D., for a court ruling
that she has satisfied the three conditions precedent to her move.  Mr. S.D.
will have two weeks after he is served to file responding material.  If the
presiding judge in Newmarket is unable to make a decision on the written
material, he or she may remit the matter to me for decision or further
direction.

Access

Prior to the move

9.      Mr. S.D.’s first access visit with the children after this
decision is released is to be exercised in the presence of a counsellor or
therapist approved by Ms. J.D.1 and the OCL.

10.    For the next four visits, Mr. S.D. will continue to exercise
access according to my order of September 14, 2016 for up to five hours of
access each week at a Supervised Access Centre or in the presence of a
professional supervisor paid by Mr. S.D..

11.    After these four visits have occurred, Mr. S.D. may resume
unsupervised visits if:

a)

No problems have been observed in the Supervised
Access Visits. For clarity, any displays of distressing emotion, such as crying
or an angry or raised voice by Mr. S.D. in the last two visits, would be considered
a problem, as would any negative discussion about Ms. J.D.1, Rabbi P.S. or this
court case or decision.

b)

He provides a letter from his therapist confirming
his regular recent attendance and that Mr. S.D. has demonstrated he appreciates
the need to avoid exposing his children to negativity about their mother, Rabbi
P.S. or this decision.

12.    Once this letter has been provided, Mr. S.D.’s following four
visits may be exercised in the community or at his home or the home of his
parents or sister. These visits will be from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. for four
consecutive Sundays.

13.    If there are no problems with these visits, Mr. S.D. may
thereafter resume unsupervised overnight visits on alternate weekends from
Friday after school to Monday return to school (or to their mother or childcare
provider, if school is not in session).

14.    The resumption of overnight contact is intended to allow Mr.
S.D. and the children as much time as possible together until the move to
England takes place.  However, if Ms. J.D.1 believes that Mr. S.D. is
continuing to expose the children to harmful behaviour during any of his
daytime or overnight access, or if she receives any more threatening or abusive
communications from him, she may unilaterally make the decision that any
further access needs to be exercised at the Supervised Access Centre until
further order of the court.

15.    If the children are being picked up or dropped off anywhere
other than from school, the pick-up and drop-off location for access shall
continue to be at a secure place as agreed upon by counsel in writing.

16.    Either party may bring an urgent motion in Newmarket, on
notice to the other side, to determine any access dispute.  If the presiding
justice feels unable to deal with the matter, he or she may try to arrange for
the motion to be scheduled before me.  However, due to difficulties in
scheduling me to preside in Newmarket, I declare that I am not seized with any
post-trial motions that either party may bring.

Access after the move to England

17.    Once the children move to England, Mr. S.D. will be entitled
to one Skype access visit with the children each Sunday. Each of the children
is to be encouraged to spend a minimum of 10 minutes on the Skype call with
their father, provided the call is not upsetting the child. The total Skype
visit shall not exceed one hour. The parties can arrange a time that will
accommodate the time difference between the two countries that will not disrupt
the children’s schedule.

18.    The parties are to exchange proposals about an access
schedule, so that the children have at least four weeks of access with their
father in Canada each year in even numbered years and five weeks of access in
odd numbered years.

19.    If the parties cannot agree on a schedule, the children are
to spend four weeks with Mr. S.D. during the summer in even numbers year. In
odd numbered years, they will spend two weeks with their father over each
December school break (or the English equivalent) and three weeks in the
summer.

20.  The summer access is not to be for a full period of three or
four consecutive weeks, unless the parties agree otherwise.  As Ms. J.D.1 has
promised that she will travel to Canada with the children in the summer, she
should ensure that the children are in Canada for at least five weeks in even
numbered years and four weeks in odd numbered years. Ms. J.D.1 will be entitled
to schedule up to seven days of time with the children at some point during the
time that they are in Canada. This will allow the children to spend time with Ms.
J.D.1’ family and will ensure that the younger children, in particular, do not
have to go for too long a period without seeing their primary caregiver. Ms.
J.D.1 may select her choice of seven days, which need not be consecutive. She
is to notify Mr. S.D. no later than May 1 each year of the dates when the
children will be with her during summer access.

21.    If Mr. S.D. is able to travel to England and arrange
accommodation, he may do so for once or twice a year and he may spend up to two
weeks with his children during each trip, provided it does not disrupt the
children’s schooling.

Child Support

22.    Mr. S.D. shall Ms. J.D.1 child support for the four children
as follows:

(a) For 2014, $340 per month on an admitted and imputed yearly
income of $18,000

(b) For 2015 and 2016, $725 per month on an admitted and imputed
yearly income of $30,000

(c) On an ongoing basis, commencing January 1, 2017, $725 per month
on an imputed income of $30,000 per year.

(d) On the first day of the month following the month in which Ms.
J.D.1 and the children move to England, Mr. S.D.’s child support obligations
shall be reduced to $600 per month support, on the basis of undue hardship.

(e) In lieu of paying full
Child Support Guideline
support, Mr.
S.D. shall be responsible for all transportation costs of the children flying
to Canada for access, as well as all of their costs while they are here. Mr.
S.D. is to continue to pay $600 per month support to Ms. J.D.1 for the children
during the time that they are visiting with him for access.

(f) Arrears
are set at $11,125 as of January 15, 2016.

(g) Arrears thereafter are to accumulate at $725 per month from
February 1, 2016  minus any payments that Mr. S.D. can prove that he has made
since that date.

Section 7 Expenses

23.    Due to the difficulties in determining the parties’ incomes, Mr.
S.D. is to continue to be responsible for one-half of their schooling costs,
including tuition, books, and uniforms, until they move to England.

24.    If the children are living outside of Canada, Mr. S.D. will
not be responsible for any further s. 7 expenses.

Spousal Support

25.    Neither party is to pay spousal support to the other. All
spousal support claims are dismissed.

Restraining Order

26.    The terms of the existing orders restraining Mr. S.D. from
contacting Ms. J.D.1 or the children, or attending at their home or school,
should be consolidated and are made final. If the parties are unable to agree
to the appropriate wording, either side may file a 14B, with a proposed draft
order, on seven days’ notice to the other party. If there is a dispute, the
responding party may file his or her own draft within a further seven days,
identifying the dispute and the reason for preferring his or her draft order.
If there is no dispute filed, the draft order will issue in the terms set out
by the person filing the original 14B. All of the terms of paragraph 761 above
shall be incorporated into the restraining order.

27.    If there is a dispute, any presiding judge in Newmarket may
make the appropriate order to settle the terms of the restraining order. If he
or she feels unable to do so, the file may be remitted to me in Barrie to deal
with the 14B.

Other Claims

28.    All other claims are dismissed.
